- If sentiment shows strong bullish (e.g., 1.00) in recent days, model tends to over-forecast; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment shows strong bearish (e.g., -1.00), model often under-forecasts; adjust downward bias or add early correction.
- After a sharp spike in price, model frequently overshoots and fails to correct — apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast by 5–10% after peak.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.00/0.25), model often drifts toward mean reversion — align forecast with recent 5–7 day average if no strong sentiment.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., after 70–75 range, price drops sharply), model tends to ignore it — add a “reversion buffer” to forecast: if price > 75, cap at 75–78; if <70, floor at 68–72.
- Model often overestimates short-term volatility after sentiment shifts — use sentiment as a volatility filter: if sentiment > 0.5, reduce forecast variance; if < -0.5, increase variance slightly.
- Forecast horizon 30d is prone to “late correction” — if true outcome shows sharp drop after day 15–20, model still holds high — adjust forecast to reflect “late correction” by reducing slope after day 18.
